{{short description|Non-linear stochastic partial differential equation}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) equation''' is a non-linear [[stochastic partial differential equation]], introduced by [[Mehran Kardar]], [[Giorgio Parisi]], and Yi-Cheng Zhang in 1986.<ref name="foo">{{cite journal|last1=Kardar|first1=Mehran|last2=Parisi|first2=Giorgio|last3=Zhang|first3=Yi-Cheng|date=3 March 1986|title=Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=56|issue=9|pages=889–892|bibcode=1986PhRvL..56..889K|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889|pmid=10033312|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233849}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{citation|first1=Martin|last1=Hairer|first2=J|last2=Quastel|year=2014|title=Weak universality of the KPZ equation|url=http://mate.dm.uba.ar/~probab/spa2014/pdf/hairer.pdf}}</ref> It describes the temporal change of a height field <math>h(\vec x,t)</math> with spatial coordinate <math>\vec x</math> and time coordinate <math>t</math>:

: <math>\frac{\partial h(\vec x,t)}{\partial t} = \nu \nabla^2 h + \frac{\lambda}{2} \left(\nabla h\right)^2 + \eta(\vec x,t) \; .</math>

Here, <math>\eta(\vec x,t)</math> is [[White noise|white]] [[Gaussian noise]] with average 

<math>\langle \eta(\vec x,t) \rangle = 0</math> 

and [[second moment]]

<math>\langle \eta(\vec x,t) \eta(\vec x',t') \rangle = 2D\delta^d(\vec x-\vec x')\delta(t-t'), </math>

<math>\nu</math>, <math>\lambda</math>, and <math>D</math> are parameters of the model, and <math>d</math> is the dimension. 

In one spatial dimension, the KPZ equation corresponds to a stochastic version of [[Burgers' equation]] with field <math>u(x,t)</math> via the substitution <math>u=-\lambda\, \partial h/\partial x</math>.

Via the [[renormalization group]], the KPZ equation is conjectured to be the [[Field theory (physics)|field theory]] of many [[surface growth]] models, such as the [[Eden growth model|Eden model]], ballistic deposition, and the weakly asymmetric single step solid on solid process (SOS) model. A rigorous proof has been given by Bertini and Giacomin in the case of the SOS model.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bertini|first1=Lorenzo|last2=Giacomin|first2=Giambattista|year=1997|title=Stochastic Burgers and KPZ equations from particle systems|journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics|volume=183|issue=3|pages=571–607|bibcode=1997CMaPh.183..571B|citeseerx=10.1.1.49.4105|doi=10.1007/s002200050044|s2cid=122139894}}</ref>

== KPZ universality class ==
Many [[interacting particle system]]s, such as the totally [[asymmetric simple exclusion process]], lie in the KPZ [[universality class]]. This class is characterized by the following [[Critical exponent|critical exponents]] in one spatial dimension (1&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 dimension): the roughness exponent <math>\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}</math>, growth exponent <math>\beta=\tfrac{1}{3}</math>, and dynamic exponent <math>z=\tfrac{3}{2}</math>. In order to check if a growth model is within the KPZ class, one can calculate the ''width'' of the surface:

: <math>W(L,t)=\left\langle\frac1L\int_0^L \big( h(x,t)-\bar{h}(t)\big)^2 \, dx\right\rangle^{1/2},</math>

where <math> \bar{h}(t) </math> is the mean surface height at time <math> t </math> and <math> L </math> is the size of the system. For models within the KPZ class, the main properties of the surface <math> h(x,t) </math> can be characterized by the [[Fereydoon Family|Family]]–[[Tamás Vicsek|Vicsek]] [[Scaling limit|scaling relation]] of the [[Hausdorff dimension|roughness]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Family|first1=F.|last2=Vicsek|first2=T.|author2-link=T. Vicsek|year=1985|title=Scaling of the active zone in the Eden process on percolation networks and the ballistic deposition model|journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General|volume=18|issue=2|pages=L75–L81|bibcode=1985JPhA...18L..75F|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/18/2/005|author1-link=F. Family}}</ref> 

: <math>
    W(L,t) \approx L^{\alpha} f(t/L^z),
</math>

with a scaling function <math alt>f(u)</math> satisfying

: <math>
    f(u) \propto \begin{cases} u^{\beta} & \ u\ll 1 \\
     1 & \ u\gg1\end{cases}
</math>

In 2014, Hairer and Quastel showed that more generally, the following KPZ-like equations lie within the KPZ universality class:<ref name=":0" />

:<math>\frac{\partial h(\vec x,t)}{\partial t} = \nu \nabla^2 h + P\left(\nabla h\right) + \eta(\vec x,t) \; ,</math>

where <math>P</math> is any even-degree [[polynomial]].

A family of processes that are conjectured to be universal limits in the (1+1) KPZ universality class and govern the long time fluctuations are the [[Airy process|Airy processes]] and the [[KPZ fixed point]].

== Solving the KPZ equation ==
Due to the [[Nonlinear system|nonlinearity]] in the equation and the presence of space-time [[white noise]], solutions to the KPZ equation are known to not be [[Smoothness|smooth]] or regular, but rather '[[fractal]]' or '[[Rough path|rough]].' Even without the nonlinear term, the equation reduces to the [[stochastic heat equation]], whose solution is not [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] in the space variable but satisfies a [[Hölder condition]] with exponent less than 1/2. Thus, the nonlinear term <math> \left(\nabla h\right)^2 </math> is [[ill-defined]] in a classical sense. 

In 2013, [[Martin Hairer]] made a breakthrough in solving the KPZ equation by an extension of the [[Cole–Hopf transformation]] and constructing approximations using [[Feynman diagram|Feynman diagrams]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hairer|first=Martin|year=2013|title=Solving the KPZ equation|journal=Annals of Mathematics|volume=178|issue=2|pages=559–664|arxiv=1109.6811|doi=10.4007/annals.2013.178.2.4|s2cid=119247908}}</ref> In 2014, he was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] for this work on the KPZ equation, along with [[Rough path|rough paths theory]] and [[regularity structures]]. There were 6 different analytic [[Self-similar solution|self-similar solutions]] found for the (1+1) KPZ equation with different analytic noise terms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barna |first1=Imre Ferenc |last2=Bognár |first2=Gabriella |last3=Mohammed |first3=Guedda |last4=Hriczó |first4=Krisztián |last5=Mátyás |first5=László |year=2020 |title=Analytic Self-Similar Solutions of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang Interface Growing Equation with Various Noise Terms |url= |journal=Mathematical Modelling and Analysis |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=241–257 |arxiv= 1904.01838|bibcode=2019arXiv190401838F |doi=10.3846/mma.2020.10459 |s2cid=102487227|doi-access=free }}</ref> 

== Physical derivation ==
A common, non-rigorous derivation begins with an attempt to model [[surface growth]] during [[crystallization]]. Let <math> h(x, t)</math> represent the height of the surface at position <math> x </math> and time <math> t </math>. The surface is expected to evolve through time according to some variant on the [[diffusion equation]], 
<math display=block>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial t }=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} h(x,t)}{\partial x^2 }\text{,}</math>
which acts to [[Smoothness|smooth]] the initial conditions.  The diffusion equation itself cannot describe the surface evolution because it is [[Deterministic system|deterministic]], omitting the effects of random [[precipitation (chemistry)|precipitation]] and dissolution.  

The simplest adaptation adds a stochastic forcing:
<math display=block>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial t }=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} h(x,t)}{\partial x^{2}}+\eta(x,t),</math> 
where <math>\eta </math> is [[Gaussian noise|Gaussian]] [[white noise]] with [[Average|mean]] zero and [[covariance]] <math display=block>E[\eta(x,t)\eta(x',t')]=\delta(x-x')\delta(t-t')\text{.}</math>  That equation is the Edwards–Wilkinson (EW) equation, also known descriptively as the [[stochastic heat equation]] with [[Additive white Gaussian noise|additive noise]]. The EW equation is mathematically tractable, being [[linear equation|linear]]; and solvable through [[Fourier analysis]].  It also exhibits an important symmetry retained in the final KPZ equation: if <math display=inline>h</math> solves the EW equation when <math display=inline>\eta</math> has mean 0, then <math display=inline>h+mt</math> also solves the EW equation when <math display=inline>\eta</math> has mean <math display=inline>m</math>.  Thus any constant terms can be added or removed from the right-hand side without modifying physical applicability.  However, the EW equation implies that fluctuations in <math display=inline>h</math> are Gaussian, which is contrary to experiment.  At least one term is missing for a physically-accurate model.<ref name=TRev>{{cite journal |last1=Tomohiro|first1=Sasamoto|title=The 1D Kardar–Parisi–Zhang equation: height distribution and universality|journal=Progress of Theoretical and Experimental Physics|year=2016|volume=2016|issue=2|article-number=022A01 |doi=10.1093/ptep/ptw002|url=https://academic.oup.com/ptep/article/2016/2/022A01/2461080 |doi-access=free|at=&sect;3.2}}</ref>  

The key observation of Kardar, Parisi, and Zhang (KPZ)<ref name="foo">{{cite journal|last1=Kardar|first1=Mehran|last2=Parisi|first2=Giorgio|last3=Zhang|first3=Yi-Cheng|date=3 March 1986|title=Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=56|issue=9|pages=889–892|bibcode=1986PhRvL..56..889K|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889|pmid=10033312|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233849}}</ref> was that the missing term depends on surface's local slope, <math display=inline>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial x }</math>  The crystal surface grows [[Normal (geometry)|normal]] to the (varying) surface, but <math display=inline>h</math> is measured along a fixed height axis.  Consequently regions with large <math display=inline>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial x }</math> have longer surface length, and see more deposition.  

One might hope that surface growth is accurately modeled through an equation of the form
<math display=block>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial t }=F\left(\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial x }\right)+ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} h(x,t)}{\partial x^{2}}+\eta(x,t) </math> 
for some function <math display=inline>F</math>.  If <math display=inline>F</math> is solely proportional to local arclength, then <math display=inline>F</math> should take (up to an additive constant, by the EW symmetry mentioned above) the value <math display=block>F(s)=\lambda\sqrt{1+s^2}\text{,}</math> for some constant <math display=inline>\lambda</math>.  However, that choice of <math display=inline>F</math> gives an intractable equation.<ref name="foog">{{cite web |title=Introduction to KPZ |first=Jeremy |last=Quastel |url=https://www.math.arizona.edu/~mathphys/school_2012/IntroKPZ-Arizona.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250407204325/https://math.arizona.edu/~mathphys/school_2012/IntroKPZ-Arizona.pdf|archive-date=7 April 2025|p=3|year=2012<!--Presumed from URL-->}}</ref>

The working physicist is now tempted by habit to simply expand <math display=inline>F</math> as a [[Maclaurin series|Taylor series about <math display=inline>0</math>]].  This Taylor expansion cannot be mathematically justified.  The function <math display=inline>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial x }</math> is large, and has very large variation: there is no convenient point to Taylor-expand around.{{sfn|Quastel|2012|pp=3,6}}  However, as discussed above, the KPZ equation is universal, in the sense that the same functions solve the KPZ equation for any <math display=inline>F(s)</math> that is a nonconstant polynomial in <math display=inline>s^2</math>.  For example, if <math display=inline>F</math> were polynomial, then one could assume it quadratic without loss of generality.  

With less rigor, one can compute that the [[renormalization group]] flow has a single fixpoint: namely, <math display=inline>F(s)=F''(0)s^2</math>.  Thus if there is an interesting model to be found, then it must behave as though <math display=inline>F(s)=F''(0)s^2</math>.<ref>Timothy Halpin-Healy and Yi-Cheng Zhang (1995). "Kinetic roughening phenomena, stochastic growth, directed polymers and all that". ''Physics Reports'', vol.&nbsp;254: p.&nbsp;236.</ref>  The KPZ equation's (extensive!) mathematical analysis is devoted to showing that the resulting equation is well-defined: ordinarily, [[tempered distribution]]s have no square, but the divergence associated with the KPZ model can be mollified after applying the Hopf-Cole transformation.{{sfn|Tomohiro|2016|at=&sect;4}}<ref>{{harvnb|Quastel|2012}}, pp.&nbsp;8-10.  "The evidence for the Hopf-Cole solutions is now overwhelming. Whatever the physicists mean by KPZ, it is them....The problem is to find an appropriate definition [or interpretation] of (1)-(3) which fits that solution and to prove the corresponding uniqueness."</ref>

For the sake of intuition, we will assume that 
<math display=block>F(s)=F'(0)+F'(0)s+\frac{1}{2}F''(0)s^{2}\text{.}</math>  
The first term can be removed from the equation by the time-shift symmetry alluded to above in the EW equation: if <math> h(x,t)</math> solves the KPZ equation, then <math> \tilde{h}(x,t):=h(x,t)-\lambda F(0)t</math> solves
<math display=block>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial t }=-\lambda F(0)+ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} h(x,t)}{\partial x^{2} }+\eta(x,t). </math>  
The second can be removed from the equation by a constant velocity shift of coordinates, since if <math> h(x,t)</math> solves the KPZ equation, then <math> \tilde{h}(x,t):=h(x- \lambda F'(0)t,t-\lambda F'(0)x)</math> solves
<math display=block>\frac{\partial \tilde{h}(x,t)}{\partial t }=-\lambda F'(0)\frac{\partial \tilde{h}(x,t)}{\partial x }+ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} \tilde{h}(x,t)}{\partial x^{2}}+\eta(x,t). </math>  
The quadratic term is the first nontrivial contribution, and it is the only one kept. We arrive at the KPZ equation 
<math display=block>\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial t }=-\lambda\left(\frac{\partial h(x,t)}{\partial x }\right)^{2} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} h(x,t)}{\partial x^{2}}+\eta(x,t). </math>
